groundTruthNarrative: Corrin Valley Transit's OTP fell from 82% to about 71% because of two April changes, not absenteeism. On 2026-04-05 the spring service change cut recovery time on 21 routes (median 15% to 8%) to free buses for a new route, so late inbound arrivals now propagate into late outbound departures. From 2026-04-20 city construction halved speeds through two work zones used by five of those routes, which became the worst performers. Routes with neither change held at about 82%. Ridership and dwell times were flat, and manual ride checks confirm the AVL OTP figures. The 40% absence rise that leadership blames is a recording artifact: ShiftLine, live on 2026-03-30, began logging partial-day absences that the paper process never recorded. Full-day absences rose only 1%, and the independent dispatch log shows missed trips, late pull-outs and extraboard use unchanged. Early leaves are higher at the garage running more recovery-cut routes, but that is cross-sectional and confounded. Disciplining every recorded occurrence would punish operators for a measurement change.

answers.rationale: At S1 the only link between absence and OTP is that both changed in April (E2, E3) plus the Director's proposed mechanism (E1) and one dispatcher anecdote (E4). The steward offers a concrete rival (layover cuts, E5) that S1 evidence cannot rule in or out, and no S1 evidence shows missed trips, pull-out delays or route-level patterns. Nothing yet counts against the claim, so 'contradicted' is not defensible, and timing alone with a live rival does not make it 'supported'.

By S3, real absence did not rise: full-day absences +1.1% (E14), missed trips for lack of an operator, late pull-outs and extraboard use all flat in the independent dispatch log (E15). Extraboard covers any route (E4), yet routes with neither recovery cuts nor construction held OTP at ~82% (E8). Late departures happen with the bus and operator present (E10). Absence cannot be the main driver.

At S1 the HR record shows a 40% rise with stable headcount (E3), the dispatcher independently reports a longer absence board and daily extraboard use (E4), and the Director agrees (E1). Even the steward does not dispute that people are absent, only why (E5). No S1 evidence questions the recording process, so the evidence taken together supports a real increase.

ShiftLine (live 2026-03-30) began recording partial-day absences that the legacy process never entered (E13); 238 of the 245-occurrence increase is that new category and full-day absences rose only 1.1% (E14). The independent, unchanged dispatch log shows no rise in uncovered work, including mid-shift reliefs (41 vs 43/day) and missed trips (E15). The 40% rise does not reflect a real attendance change.

At S1 the layover claim rests only on the steward's account (E5), countered only by the Director's second-hand statement that running times are fine (E1). No schedule document or route-level data is available yet. The claim is live but undiscriminated.

By S2, recovery was cut on 21 routes on 2026-04-05 while running times were unchanged (E6), which explains the Director's 'running times are fine' (E1). Recovery-cut routes without construction fell 81.6% to 71.5% while unchanged routes held at 82.3% to 81.7%, stepping down in the week of 2026-04-06 (E8). Late first-timepoint departures on those routes tripled and 81% followed a late inbound arrival with bus and operator present (E10). Ridership and dwell are flat (E11).

Lane reductions began 2026-04-20 (E7); the five corridor routes took a second, larger step down that week and fell to 52.5% versus 71.5% for recovery-cut routes off the corridors (E8); work-zone segment times roughly doubled while other segments of the same routes were unchanged (E9). The Director's 'a few blocks' dismissal (E1) is countered by data.
Boardings fell slightly (61,200 to 60,400) and median dwell is unchanged at 18 s (E11); unchanged routes held OTP (E8). The evidence counts against ridership/dwell as a driver.

Trap: the absence metric is an artifact, but the OTP metric is not. Its definition and AVL equipment are unchanged since 2023 (E2), independent stopwatch ride checks agree with AVL at 97% of timepoints and give 72% vs 73% OTP (E12), and the decline is localized to routes with specific operational changes (E8, E9, E10), which a reporting artifact would not produce.

At S1 recorded absences and OTP move together from April (E2, E3), so they are associated, but the only mechanism is asserted (E1, one anecdote in E4) and a co-timed rival (the spring schedule change, E5) is unaddressed. Causation is not established; there is enough to call it more than 'unknown'.

The recorded rise is produced by the new recording system (E13, E14), and the operational channels through which absence could affect OTP - missed trips, late pull-outs, extraboard use - are unchanged (E15). Routes covered by the same extraboard but without schedule or construction changes kept their OTP (E4, E8). Evidence counts against the link.

Temporal order (cut 2026-04-05, step in week of 04-06), a comparison group (unchanged routes, same period, both garages, flat), a specific mechanism (late inbound arrivals propagating into late departures with no recovery, E10), and rivals excluded (ridership E11, measurement E12, absence E15).

The step for the corridor routes coincides with the 2026-04-20 lane reductions, separate from the 04-06 schedule step (E7, E8); segment times double only inside the work zones (E9); corridor routes fall far below recovery-cut routes without construction (E8). Timing, localization and comparison establish causation for the incremental decline.

Operators assigned to recovery-cut routes have higher early-leave rates than those on other routes (18 vs 10 per 100, pooled across garages; North 19 vs South 11, E16), consistent with the steward's account (E5), so the two are associated. But there is no pre-April baseline, operators on cut routes are older and the cut routes are longer (E16), and mid-shift reliefs barely changed (E15). Co-occurrence without established causation; not 'unknown', because the association is shown at operator-assignment level.

ShiftLine went live 2026-03-30, immediately before the April jump (E3, E13); it records a category the old process did not (E13); that new category accounts for 238 of the 245 increase while full-day absences are flat (E14); the independent dispatch log shows no real change (E15). Mechanism, timing and decomposition establish causation.

At S1 absence appears to have risen (E3) but whether it drives OTP is unestablished (E1 vs E5). Discipline would be justified only if absence were confirmed as the cause; committing now is premature. It is not yet 'harmful' because nothing at S1 shows the occurrences are mis-measured.

By S3 the policy would count every ShiftLine occurrence (E17), including partial-day absences that were never counted before (E13, E14), punishing operators for a recording change. It targets a non-cause (E15, E8) and would fall hardest on operators assigned to the recovery-cut routes (E16). It punishes the wrong party and leaves OTP unaddressed.

At S1 the layover hypothesis rests on the steward's claim alone (E5) against the Director's account (E1). Restoring recovery time would be right if the claim were confirmed, but at S1 it is not, and the change costs buses and service.

With all evidence, the recovery cut is an established cause of the decline on 21 routes (E6, E8, E10). Restoring it targets the main mechanism directly; the trade-off with Route 51 is explicit (E6) and a decision for leadership, but restoring recovery is among the best next actions.

The construction effect is causal and will persist until August 2027 (E7), with the work-zone segment times measured (E9) and the corridor routes the worst performers (E8). Schedules that reflect actual construction-period running times and work-zone traffic management address a cause the agency cannot remove.
The attendance report presents a recording change as a 40% rise (E3, E13, E14) and is about to drive a Board policy decision (E17). Correcting it is low-cost and prevents a harmful decision.

The OTP measure is unchanged since 2023 and independently validated by ride checks (E2, E12). Suspending publication would withhold accurate performance information from the Board and public while a real decline continues (E8).

With all evidence the decline is decomposed by route group with comparison groups and mechanisms (E8, E9, E10), rivals are excluded (E11, E12), and the absence explanation is refuted (E14, E15). This is enough to commit to substantive interventions (restoring recovery, construction-period schedules). The only open question (R4) does not affect them.
